meta.subtitle: A defense growth story riding a spending supercycle, priced for it even after a fall by two-thirds, with the payoff still years of investment away

analystSentiment.commentary:
Kratos is a defense contractor the market has repriced hard: the shares are $47.62 against a 52-week range of $43.09 – $134.00, down by roughly two-thirds from the top, yet the operating momentum has gone the other way. Second-quarter revenue was $458.8 million, up 30.5% and 19.1% organically, and the bookings, backlog and pipeline the growth section details all point up. Management raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $1.750 to $1.810 billion and forecasts organic growth of 18% to 23%, and the Street is nearly unanimous: 22 Buys, 3 Holds, no Sells, and a consensus target of $98.15, +106.1% above the price.

We are positive but not that positive. We rate the shares BUY with a target range of $43–$72, below the Street, because the two things holding the stock down are real. Kratos earns almost nothing today on $1.3B of revenue, so the trailing and forward multiples the valuation section lays out are extreme, a growth multiple even on out-year consensus earnings. And it is deliberately consuming cash to grow: the cash-flow section details FY25's free-cash-flow burn and the further use guided for 2026.

What tips the balance to BUY is the setup beneath the multiple. The balance sheet is net cash, the backlog and pipeline are at the levels the financials and growth sections detail, the demand is a policy-driven recapitalization rather than a cycle Kratos must create, and the price already sits a hair above its 52-week low. The probability-weighted fair value of $58.50 is a low-twenties percentage above the price; the distance to the Street is the discount we take for a valuation that leaves no room for a stumble.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Kratos Defense & Security Solutions is a San Diego-based contractor to the U.S. government and its allies, organized in two segments: Kratos Government Solutions, which spans satellite and space command-and-control software, microwave electronics, C5ISR, turbine and jet-engine technologies, and defense and rocket support; and Unmanned Systems, which builds jet-powered drones led by the Valkyrie. The company describes its strategy as being first to market with hardware and software engineered up front for affordable, high-volume production, acting as a low-cost prime where its probability of winning is high and as a merchant supplier of subsystems to the large primes elsewhere. It has more than 700 employees in Israel in its microwave-electronics and SATCOM business, and it reports in a fiscal year ending in late December.

The growth is concentrated in a few areas management points to repeatedly: hypersonic and rocket systems, jet engines for cruise missiles and drones, and space and satellite communications. On the June quarter's segment detail, Government Solutions was $379.7 million of revenue at 22.0% organic growth and Unmanned Systems $79.1 million at 8.1%, with the sharpest growth inside Government Solutions in defense rocket support, turbine technologies and microwave products.

The vendor's revenue split is by kind rather than by segment: FY25 Product was 65.2% of revenue ($877.8M) and Service 34.8% ($469M), and the moat section reads those two lines. By geography, the United States was 79.1% of FY25 revenue, with Europe at 5.8%, Asia Pacific 5.3%, the Middle East 4.9% and smaller balances elsewhere. The demand backdrop is policy: the MD&A cites the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and a multi-year step-up in national-security spending that the systemic-risk section quantifies.

thesis.label: BUY
thesis.body:
The thesis is that Kratos is a real beneficiary of a defense recapitalization, sold at a price that already assumes it. The demand is not in doubt: the bookings, backlog and pipeline the growth section lays out all point up, as does organic growth guided to 18% to 23% for 2026 (the formal press-release range; the earnings-call transcript gives 19% to 23%, and we rely on the press-release figure), and the balance sheet is net cash, so Kratos can self-fund the build-out without the solvency risk that dogs other fast growers. The stock has fallen by roughly two-thirds from its 52-week high, which has taken some of the excess out of the price.

What keeps us below the Street is the valuation against the earnings. On a company that earns almost nothing today and is guided to keep using cash in 2026, the trailing and EBITDA multiples the valuation section sets out price years of flawless execution. The margin is thin and, in the quarter, negative at the operating line, and roughly 70% of the contract base is fixed-price, which caps the upside from inflation while exposing the downside. Our BUY rests on the growth and the balance sheet clearing a lower bar than consensus sets; the bear case is a de-rating if the appropriations cycle stalls or the margin ramp slips, and the shares have shown they can fall a long way.

catalysts: The hypersonics ramp: management's own trajectory has this business roughly tripling over two years, and the growth section carries the figures and the funding behind them.

The jet-engine build-out: initial orders are placed for thousands of low-cost turbojet engines for cruise-missile programs, with the growth section detailing the volumes and the second facility with GE Aerospace.
Margin inflection: management guides adjusted EBITDA margin to expand as production scales and fixed-cost leverage improves; the financials section says what would confirm it.

Appropriations turning into orders: the national-security budget and the larger FY2027 request the systemic-risk section quantifies are the funding pool the backlog draws from, and that section also carries the timing risk.
Free cash flow turning: the investment phase depresses cash today, so any sign of it easing is the catalyst the cash-flow section is watching.
risks: Valuation: the multiple prices years of execution, so a growth or margin stumble compresses it hard; the valuation section carries the math.
Negative free cash flow: the investment phase means cash is guided to keep flowing out through 2026, and the cash-flow section carries the size.
Fixed-price margin squeeze: most of the contract base is fixed-price, so inflation and labor cost the company rather than the customer; the financials section carries the effect.
Government funding: shutdowns, continuing resolutions and appropriations delays can push orders and cash, a risk the MD&A dwells on and the risk section carries.
The shekel: a strong Israeli shekel is already denting profitability in the microwave business, and the risk section carries the quantified drag.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended late December.

financials.incomeCommentary:
The income statement is the story of a company spending its margin to buy growth. Revenue climbed steadily from $0.8B in FY21 to $1.3B in FY25, with the growth rate accelerating to +18.5% in the latest year, and the second quarter carried it further, up 30.5% to $458.8 million with 19.1% organic growth after the Nomad and Orbit acquisitions. What has not followed is profit. Gross margin has drifted down from 27.7% in FY21 to 22.1% in FY25, and operating margin has hovered near breakeven throughout, 3.4% at the start of the series and 2.1% by FY25; in the June quarter the company reported an operating loss of $1.6 million even as revenue grew, and non-operating income carried it to net income of $4.4 million and diluted EPS of $0.02. FY25 net income was $22M and diluted EPS $0.13, a clearly positive full year after losses as recent as FY22 and FY23.

Management's preferred measure tells the intended trajectory: adjusted EBITDA was $38.2 million in the quarter, above the guided $30 million to $35 million, and the company frames current margins as suppressed by choice. The quarter carried $16.3 million of non-cash stock compensation, $13.6 million of company-funded research and development and $12.5 million of amortization, and a strong Israeli shekel cut adjusted EBITDA by $2.5 million. The line to watch is whether the guided margin expansion, roughly 100 basis points of adjusted EBITDA margin a year, arrives as the hypersonics, engine and space volumes scale, or whether thin fixed-price margins and cost inflation keep the reported operating line near zero.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended late December.

financials.balanceCommentary:
The balance sheet is the strongest part of the story and the reason the downside is a de-rating rather than a solvency event. FY25 total equity was $2.0B, up from $1.4B a year earlier and far beyond what a year of net income could build, so the company has funded itself with stock rather than debt. Total debt fell to $145.8M and net debt was -$414.8M, a net cash position, with the current ratio at 4.06 for the year and 5.54 on a trailing basis. Trailing net debt to EBITDA of -10.5x and interest coverage of 5.2x both reflect the same fact: leverage is not the constraint here.

That matters because the growth plan is capital-hungry. The company is buying long-lead components and building facilities ahead of contract awards, which the MD&A lists at length, from a hypersonic integration facility in Indiana to jet-engine plants in Michigan and Oklahoma and expanded microwave-electronics facilities in Israel. A net-cash balance sheet lets Kratos place those bets without raising expensive debt or being forced to stop mid-build, and the highlight cells show the net cash and the current ratio alongside the investment it funds. The counter is that the equity funding dilutes existing holders, and share count has risen as the company has issued stock to keep the balance sheet ahead of the spend; a reader paying a multiple this rich on earnings this thin is also paying for more shares than a year ago.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended late December.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
Cash flow is where the investment phase is most visible. Operating cash flow has bounced around zero across the five years, and free cash flow has been negative in four of them, at -$137.4M in FY25 for a free-cash-flow margin of -10.2%, the weakest in the series. The June quarter used $11.0 million in operations and $18.9 million of free cash flow after $17.2 million of capital expenditure, with management attributing the outflow to working capital for the revenue ramp, receivables, and prepayments for long-lead materials rather than to losses.

The guidance makes the near-term shape explicit and negative: 2026 capital expenditure of $125 million to $135 million and a full-year free-cash-flow use of $85 million to $105 million, with total forecasted investments of $250 million to $275 million once working-capital items such as the rocket-motor inventory build and the jet-engine component orders are included. Management frames all of this as deliberate, front-loaded spending to capture programs that pay out later, and the net-cash balance sheet the balance-sheet section describes is what makes it affordable. Our judgment on cash is that the strategy is coherent and the timing is the risk: the market will not pay for the backlog indefinitely while cash flows out, so the date free cash flow turns positive matters as much as the growth rate, and the pack does not put that date sooner than beyond 2027.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
Kratos cannot be valued on current earnings without the number looking absurd, and that is the heart of the debate. The trailing P/E is 277.0x, EV/EBITDA is 64.9x and price-to-sales is 5.9x, multiples that only make sense as a claim on future scale; the forward P/E on next-twelve-month estimates is 56.8x and on FY27E consensus EPS of $1.13 it is about 42.2x, still a growth multiple for a defense contractor. The company pays no dividend. Consensus revenue reaches $1.8B in FY26E and $2.2B in FY27E, so the market is paying for a revenue base it expects to grow by roughly two-thirds from FY25 to FY27E, with margins expanding as it does; peers are pending a peer data source, so we cannot place the multiple against other defense names here.

The Street is close to unanimous and far above the price: 25 analysts, 22 Buys, 3 Holds and no Sells, a consensus target of $98.15 (+106.1%), a median of $100.00 and a range of $74.00–$135.00 whose very low end still sits well above today's $47.62. Even the most cautious published target implies upside, which is unusual and tells you the sell side treats the drawdown as an entry point. Our view is more measured: the growth and the balance sheet justify a BUY, but a multiple this high on earnings this thin, with free cash flow negative, warrants a target below the Street and a wide range, because the same multiple that lifts the shares in the bull case is what compresses them in the bear.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The recapitalization plays out: hypersonics, engines and space scale as management describes, organic growth holds in the high teens to low twenties, adjusted EBITDA margin expands about 100 basis points a year, free cash flow turns toward positive, and the market re-rates the shares toward the Street's consensus as the backlog converts.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Guidance is met: revenue of $1.750 to $1.810 billion in 2026 and continued high-teens organic growth into 2027, with margins improving slowly, but the multiple stays capped while free cash flow is still negative, so the shares gain only modestly from a price already near the low of their range.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Appropriations stall through a shutdown or continuing resolution, the fixed-price margin squeeze and shekel drag persist, the investment phase keeps free cash flow negative longer than planned, and a multiple built on future earnings compresses hard, taking the shares below their 52-week low.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
We weight the Base case at 45%, the Bull at 30% and the Bear at 25%, for a probability-weighted fair value of $58.50, a low-twenties percentage above the price and inside the BUY envelope; the $43–$72 target range brackets the Base. The Base case is guidance delivered with the multiple staying where valuation discipline caps it while cash still flows out, which from a price near the 52-week low is a modest gain. The Bull case is the supercycle converting the backlog into scale and margin, and a re-rating toward the Street's consensus; we give it three chances in ten because the demand is real but the re-rating needs free cash flow to turn, which the pack does not yet show. The Bear case carries a full quarter of the weight because the valuation gives the shares a long way to fall, and defense appropriations have a history of the delays the MD&A catalogs.

A move to STRONG BUY would need free cash flow to turn positive on schedule and the hypersonics and engine ramps to show up in the reported numbers, not just the backlog. A move to HOLD would follow a cut to organic growth or margin guidance, a further slip in the free-cash-flow timeline, or an appropriations breakdown that pushes orders out of the model.

segments.name: Product
segments.body: Product was 65.2% of FY25 revenue, $877.8M, and it is where the growth and the investment concentrate. This is the hardware Kratos designs for affordable mass production: jet drones led by the Valkyrie, small turbojet and turbofan engines for cruise missiles, hypersonic vehicles and Zeus and Oriole solid rocket motors, microwave electronics, and space and satellite systems. The June quarter's fast-growing lines sit here, with defense rocket support up 50.2%, turbine technologies up 43.3% and microwave products up 29.5% organically. The moat in Product is a first-to-market, low-cost manufacturing position that management pitches as a differentiator both to the large primes it supplies and to the government as a prime itself; the vulnerability is that most of it is fixed-price, so margins depend on holding cost as volumes ramp, and roughly 70% of the total contract base carries that risk. This is the segment funding the facilities the cash-flow section describes, and its returns arrive only as those plants fill.

segments.name: Service
segments.body: Service was 34.8% of FY25 revenue, $469M, and it is the steadier, stickier half. It covers the software and support that wrap the hardware: virtualized ground systems and command-and-control and telemetry software for satellites, the OpenSpace platform, training systems, and defense and rocket support services. Recurring software and support revenue carries higher and more durable margins than build-to-print hardware, and the space and satellite command-and-control business is one management calls its largest and describes as rapidly growing, with expected margin expansion as space becomes a contested domain. The counter is that services grow more slowly than the hardware ramp that dominates the headline numbers, so as a share of revenue this steadier base is being diluted by the faster, thinner-margin Product growth rather than leading the mix. It is the ballast in the model rather than the engine.

moatFactors.name: Incumbent programs and backlog
moatFactors.body: Defense revenue is protected by the difficulty of dislodging an incumbent once a system is an established program, and Kratos is converting bookings into that position, with the book-to-bill, bookings and backlog the growth section lays out and much of that backlog already funded. Backlog and multi-year programs give revenue visibility competitors cannot quickly take. The counter, which the 10-K states plainly, is that backlog is an uncertain indicator: the company may not receive the full amounts, and government contracts can be delayed or cancelled without penalty, so the moat is real only for programs that actually get funded and fielded.

moatFactors.name: Affordable mass production
moatFactors.body: Kratos's stated edge is being first to market with hardware engineered up front for low-cost, high-volume manufacturing, the model behind the plan to build 3,000 turbojet engines in 2027 at roughly $50,000 each and to produce Valkyries at scale. In a market the Pentagon wants filled with affordable mass rather than exquisite one-offs, that positioning is a genuine differentiator, and management frames it as a value-add to the primes it supplies. The counter is that low-cost manufacturing is a cost position, not a patent: it must be re-earned every year against competition the 10-K describes as intense, from larger primes and from new defense-technology entrants.

moatFactors.name: Specialized facilities and clearances
moatFactors.body: Much of what Kratos does requires capital, security clearances and facilities that take years to build: classified program spaces, a hypersonic integration facility, solid-rocket-motor and jet-engine plants, and a space-qualified microwave-electronics facility. Those, plus more than 700 employees in Israel with access to battle-proven systems, are hard for a new entrant to replicate quickly. The counter is that these are also the source of the cash burn and the fixed-cost base: the same specialization that keeps rivals out keeps margins thin until the facilities are full, and skilled-labor shortages the 10-K names make staffing them a persistent challenge.

moatFactors.name: Merchant-supplier position
moatFactors.body: Kratos positions itself as the merchant supplier of subsystems, engines and electronics to the whole defense complex, selling to the large primes and the new entrants alike rather than only competing with them. That breadth spreads its bets across programs and customers. The counter is that a merchant supplier has limited pricing power: it sits between powerful customers and its own supply chain, its customer relationships are concentrated in a few large accounts, and the 10-K flags that the loss or delay of a top customer or program would hurt. It is a sensible place to stand in an arms build-out, but it is not a position that commands premium economics on its own.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is narrow: durable enough to protect revenue that is already contracted, not wide enough to command the margins the valuation implies. What lasts is the installed base of programs, the clearances and specialized plants, and a low-cost manufacturing reputation that fits what the Pentagon says it wants; those give Kratos years of visible work and a seat at the programs being funded now. What does not last on its own is pricing power, because most contracts are fixed-price and competition is intense, and the demand itself is a policy choice that a future budget can reverse. The widening path is the shift toward software, space command-and-control and recurring content, and toward becoming the entrenched second source on high-volume munitions and engines; the narrowing path is a return to peacetime budgets or a margin structure that never thickens despite scale. We rate the moat narrow because the franchise clearly protects the backlog it has and does not clearly earn the returns the multiple assumes.

points: Bookings lead revenue: a last-twelve-month book-to-bill of 1.3 to 1.0 on $1.990 billion of bookings, a $2.084 billion backlog and a $15.0 billion pipeline, with management guiding third-quarter organic growth of 19% to 25% and fourth-quarter growth of 19% to 31%. The counter is that the 10-K calls backlog an uncertain indicator of future results.

Hypersonics is the designated engine: management puts the business at roughly $200 million of revenue in 2025, tracking to $400 million in 2026 and at least $700 million in 2027, backed by about $400 million of recently received hypersonic and other funding and a MACH-TB program the department's documents size near $7 billion over five years.

Jet engines scale next: Kratos is ordering components for 3,000 small turbojet engines for 2027 and an additional 5,000 for 2028 at roughly $50,000 each, aimed at cruise-missile programs, plus a turbofan facility in Oklahoma with GE Aerospace for larger munitions, an opportunity management sizes in the tens of thousands of engines.

Government Solutions is carrying the quarter, up 22.0% organically to $379.7 million, and its last-twelve-month book-to-bill is 1.4 to 1.0, while Unmanned Systems grew 8.1% to $79.1 million and is guided to about 10% organic growth for the year on Valkyrie awards, with roughly 40 Valkyries a year planned from 2028.

The funding backdrop is the tailwind: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and the step-up in national-security spending the systemic-risk section quantifies name Golden Dome, space, unmanned systems and missiles as priorities Kratos serves. The counter is that these are appropriations subject to Congress, not orders in hand.

Consensus already embeds much of this: revenue of $1.8B in FY26E and $2.2B in FY27E and EPS of $0.84 then $1.13, so the growth debate is less whether revenue compounds than whether margin and cash follow it.

management.leadership: Eric DeMarco has been President and Chief Executive Officer through the company's long transformation from a security-services roll-up into a defense-technology manufacturer, and Deanna Lund is Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer; the April 2026 proxy classifies both as non-independent by virtue of their roles, alongside three operational division presidents named as executive officers. The record supports the strategy's execution: FY25 revenue grew to $1.347 billion at 16.6% organic growth, exceeding the company's own $1.330 billion goal, and adjusted EBITDA rose from $105.7 million in 2024 to $119.9 million in 2025 even while the company absorbed inflation on its fixed-price base. The reservation is that management is asking shareholders to fund a multi-year investment phase on faith in programs not yet awarded, and to pay a high multiple while free cash flow is negative; that is a defensible strategy in a recapitalization, but it concentrates a great deal in the judgment that the awards and the margin expansion arrive on the timeline described.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is single-minded: internally funded investment ahead of contract awards, financed by equity rather than debt. The company is buying long-lead components and building facilities across hypersonics, engines, microwave electronics and space, with FY26 capital expenditure guided to $125 million to $135 million and, once working-capital items are counted, the larger total investment envelope the cash-flow section sets out, including a $40 million to $45 million rocket-motor inventory build and $50 million to $55 million for the Prometheus joint venture with RAFAEL. There are no dividends and no buybacks, which is right for a company at this stage. The funding choice keeps the balance sheet net cash, as the balance-sheet section describes, but it dilutes: equity has grown well beyond retained earnings, so per-share value depends on the investments earning more than the new shares cost. Our judgment is that the allocation is coherent with the opportunity and that its discipline will be tested by whether these bets convert to funded programs before the market tires of the cash outflow.
management.governance: The April 2026 proxy describes a conventional board: nine directors, seven of them independent under Nasdaq rules, with only the CEO and CFO non-independent, and an audit committee of independent directors that reviews related-party transactions. The company states it engaged in no related-party transactions requiring disclosure in fiscal 2025, and it runs a say-on-pay vote and benchmarks pay against peers. For 2025 the proxy describes goals balanced across organic revenue growth, increased adjusted EBITDA and margin expansion together with increasing operating cash flow generation, so the stated priorities line up with the operating goals the report tracks, cash generation included. The excerpt gives the goals the compensation committee weighed rather than the incentive-plan metrics and weights, and it carries the board composition, the independence determinations and the related-party policy but not the full pay tables, so we make no claim on how pay is structured or on the quantum of executive pay. Governance here is unremarkable in the good sense: no control structure, no dual-class shares, and a board that is majority independent.
management.insiderOwnership: Insider ownership is modest, which is typical for a company this size but worth naming given how much the thesis rests on management's judgment. As of March 20, 2026, on 187,333,628 shares outstanding, CEO Eric DeMarco held 1,123,927 shares, less than one percent, and all directors and executive officers as a group of 17 people held 2,826,938 shares, 1.5%. The top disclosed holder is BlackRock at 21,491,945 shares, 11.5%, an index-scale position rather than a strategic one. The pattern is a professionally managed, widely held company in which insiders are aligned to the share price through equity awards more than through large owned stakes, and in which no single holder or founder controls the vote. There is no super-voting class and no controlling shareholder, so public holders own both the economics and, collectively, the control.

idiosyncratic: Valuation risk dominates. On the trailing, EBITDA and out-year multiples the valuation section sets out, the shares price years of execution, so a growth or margin disappointment compresses the multiple from a great height; the stock's fall from $134.00 to $47.62 over the past year is a live demonstration of how far that can go. The net-cash balance sheet means the downside is a de-rating rather than an impairment, but a de-rating from this multiple is severe.

Free cash flow stays negative. The financials section details FY25's free-cash-flow burn, the further use guided for 2026 and the total investment envelope behind it, so the company will consume cash through at least 2026 and, on its own language, into 2027. Equity funding keeps it solvent but dilutes holders, and the market's patience for backlog without cash is finite.

Fixed-price contracts and cost inflation. Roughly 70% of the contract base is fixed-price, so inflation in materials, parts and skilled labor is Kratos's cost to absorb until contracts renew, which the proxy says has held margins down on longer-term production work. A skilled-labor and security-clearance shortage the 10-K flags makes staffing the new plants harder and dearer.

The shekel and international exposure. A strong Israeli shekel reduced adjusted EBITDA by $2.5 million in the quarter and $2.8 million over six months, because the microwave business is paid in dollars but pays its 700-plus Israeli staff in shekels; the same operations sit in a region whose conflict the company both supplies into and is exposed to.

Customer and program concentration. The 10-K warns that the loss or delay of a top customer or program would hurt results, and Kratos's growth leans heavily on a handful of programs, hypersonics, engines and space, several of them not yet awarded or dependent on classified customers the company cannot discuss until revenue appears.
risks.systemic: The systemic exposure is the U.S. defense budget and the process that funds it. Kratos's demand rests on a recapitalization the MD&A quantifies, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's $156 billion, a FY2026 national-security spend near $1 trillion and a FY2027 request of $1.5 trillion, but appropriations are a political process, and the same MD&A dwells on continuing resolutions, debt-ceiling fights and government shutdowns that delay orders and payments; a shutdown and extended continuing resolution in late 2025 and early 2026 already pushed funding. The mechanism for a contractor is direct: budgets set the size of the pool, and procurement reform and shifting administration priorities set who gets paid from it, both of which can move faster than the multi-year facilities Kratos is building. Broader macro conditions add supply-chain disruption, including electronics and memory pulled toward AI data centers, and cost inflation the company cannot fully pass through. The offset is that a deteriorating geopolitical backdrop, the very reason for the recapitalization, tends to sustain defense spending across administrations, so the systemic risk is one of timing and mix more than of the demand disappearing.

body: **BUY, target range $43–$72.** Kratos sits in the middle of a defense recapitalization with the bookings, backlog and pipeline to show for it, a balance sheet that is net cash, and a share price that has already fallen by roughly two-thirds from its high to a hair above its 52-week low. That combination of real, funded demand and a beaten-down price is what earns the BUY, and a probability-weighted fair value of $58.50 that sits a low-twenties percentage above the price.

We stop short of the Street's $98.15 because the valuation still asks a lot. On the trailing and EBITDA multiples the valuation section sets out, on a company earning almost nothing today and guiding to negative free cash flow through 2026, the price already pays for the hypersonics, engine and space ramps to arrive and to carry margins with them. The growth we believe; the multiple leaves no margin for the timing slipping, which in defense it often does.

The conditions that would move the rating up to STRONG BUY or down to HOLD are set out in the valuation section; in short, the rating rises when the cash flow turns as promised and the programs reach reported earnings, and it falls if the growth, margin or funding story cracks.
